Summary

Add the ability for the oncall-agent-api to create Pull Requests in {{artemishealth/deployments}} so that when a change is requested via Teams, the agent can propose K8s manifest changes through a PR. ArgoCD auto-syncs after merge.
The oncall-agent-api currently has read-only GitHub capabilities (search deployments, get commits). This feature enables a GitOps workflow where the agent can:
h1. Diagnose an issue using K8s tools
h1. Discover and read the relevant manifest files from {{artemishealth/deployments}}
h1. Propose YAML changes and present a diff to the user
h1. After explicit user approval, create a PR with the changes
h1. ArgoCD auto-syncs after human review and merge

A reference implementation exists targeting a homelab repo ({{arigsela/kubernetes}} with single {{base-apps/}} path). This implementation adapts it for production with _multi-path support_ ({{crossplane-services/}} and {{infrastructure/}}).

column1: The oncall-agent-api has been enhanced with GitHub GitOps capabilities and deployed to _prod-eks_. The agent can now read manifests from and create Pull Requests in {{artemishealth/deployments}}.
_ _{{get_gitops_file}}* — Read any manifest file from {{artemishealth/deployments}} (crossplane-services/ or infrastructure/)
_ _{{list_gitops_directory}}* — Discover manifest files and directory structure for any service
_ _{{create_remediation_pr}}* — Create a PR with proposed K8s manifest changes (requires explicit user approval via Teams)
_Service-to-folder mapping_ populated in the agent's system prompt from the actual repo structure:
* {{crossplane-services/}} — Crossplane-managed resources organized by cluster (dev-eks, prod-eks, test-eks)
* Fine-grained GitHub PAT scoped to specific repos and minimal permissions (Contents R/W, Pull Requests R/W, Actions Read)
* Multi-path allowlist: only {{crossplane-services/}} and {{infrastructure/}} are accessible
* Path traversal prevention via {{os.path.normpath}} with directory boundary enforcement
* No delete operations — only {{update}} and {{create}} actions allowed
* Atomic commits via Git Data API (single commit per PR, no partial failures)
* Agent requires explicit user confirmation in Teams before creating any PR
* PRs labeled {{oncall-agent}} + {{automated}} for easy filtering — no auto-merge
h3. How to Test via Teams
h1. Ask the agent: _""List the manifest files for the oncall-agent service in the deployments repo""_
h1. Ask: _""Show me the current deployment manifest for oncall-agent in dev-eks""_
h1. Ask: _""The oncall-agent needs its log level changed from DEBUG to INFO. Can you create a PR for that?""_
h1. Agent will show the diff and ask for confirmation — say ""yes"" to create the PR
h1. Verify the PR appears in {{artemishealth/deployments}} with correct branch naming and labels

Overview

Add the ability to exclude specific CVEs from active reporting in the EKS CVE Monitor. Exclusions are stored in AWS Secrets Manager as a simple JSON array, allowing updates without rebuilding the container image.

CVEs like OpenSSL CMS parsing (CVE-2025-15467) exist in images but the vulnerable code paths are never exercised in n8n's architecture. These should be excluded from active reporting to reduce noise and focus on actionable vulnerabilities.
AWS Secrets Manager                    EKS CVE Monitor
* {{scripts/apply_exclusions.py}} - Python script to process exclusions from env var
* {{scripts/run_scan.sh}} - Added step 5/5 to apply exclusions after scan, updated Teams notification with Excluded column
* {{k8s/cronjob.yaml}} - Added CVE_EXCLUSIONS env var from cve-monitor-config secret
* {{PROMPT.md}} and {{PROMPT-hybrid.md}} - Updated generate_report task to include exclusions section
h1. ExternalSecret syncs exclusion list from AWS Secrets Manager to pod env var
h1. After Trivy scans, script filters out excluded CVEs
h1. Report shows excluded CVEs in separate section
h1. To update: modify secret in AWS, re-run CronJob (no image rebuild)
* (/) CVE exclusions can be managed via AWS Secrets Manager without image rebuild
* (/) Excluded CVEs appear in separate ""Excluded CVEs"" section in report
* (/) Executive summary shows active vs excluded counts

Overview
Research feasibility and create POC for adding AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of the SFTP server to enable target group management, load balancing, and future high availability.
The current SFTP infrastructure uses a single EC2 instance with an Elastic IP directly attached. This SPIKE investigates adding an NLB layer to:
* Enable target group management for easier instance replacement
* Prepare infrastructure for multi-instance high availability
h3. Can NLB Send SFTP Traffic to EC2?
NLB operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), making it ideal for SFTP:
* TCP protocol support - SFTP uses raw TCP on port 22
* Connection persistence - NLB maintains TCP connection state for SFTP sessions
* No protocol inspection - Unlike ALB, NLB doesn't inspect application-layer protocols
* Multi-port support - Can create listeners for ports 22 and 22422
Key finding: AWS NLB supports Elastic IP assignment. The existing EIP can be moved from EC2 to NLB with zero vendor impact:
* Vendors with IP whitelisting don't need to change anything
* DNS-based connections continue working (Route53 points to same EIP)
* Source IP is preserved in logs (NLB preserves client IP with instance targets)

When scaling to multiple instances, SSH host keys must be synchronized across all instances to avoid client verification warnings. This can be achieved by syncing {{/etc/ssh/ssh_host_*}} keys via EFS.

Overview
Rotate the artemis-auth RSA keypair used by Keycloak for signing JWT tokens and SSO cookies. This rotation uses a _blue/green approach_ to ensure zero session loss during the transition.

{info}Keycloak natively supports blue/green key rotation by allowing multiple active keys with different priorities. New tokens are signed with the highest priority key, while old tokens can still be verified with lower priority keys.{info}

column3: Create new RSA key (green) with higher priority
Both keys active - green signs, blue verifies

column1: _ _New key (green)* - Higher priority (e.g., 200), used for signing all new tokens and cookies
_ _Old key (blue)_ - Lower priority (e.g., 100), remains active for _verification only*
* As users authenticate or refresh tokens, they naturally migrate to green-signed tokens
* After sufficient migration period (1-2 months), blue key can be safely removed
h3. Phase 1: Create New RSA Key (Preprod First)
h1. Log into Keycloak Admin Console
h1. Set _Priority_ higher than existing key (e.g., if current is 100, set new to 200)
h1. Verify new key appears in _Active keys_ tab with highest priority
h1. Monitor authentication logs for any issues
h1. Confirm new tokens are being signed with new key (check JWT header {{kid}} value)
h1. Wait 30-60 days for natural token migration
h1. Click on old key provider
h1. Toggle _Active_ to _Off_ (makes key passive - can still verify but won't sign)
h1. Wait additional 1-2 weeks to ensure no issues
h1. Toggle _Enabled_ to _Off_ or delete the provider
If issues occur with the new key:
h1. Increase priority of old (blue) key above new key
h1. Or disable the new (green) key provider
h1. New tokens will immediately use the old key again
h1. Generate new key immediately (steps above)
h1. Push _not-before_ policy to invalidate existing tokens:
h2. Click _Push_ to notify all clients
{warning}Pushing not-before policy will force all users to re-authenticate immediately.{warning}
_ Remove old keys _1-2 months* after creating new ones
* Document rotation dates for audit trail

Overview
Update DMARC DNS record for artemishealth.com to strengthen email security. Per SEC team guidance, implementing _quarantine @ 100%_ as an intermediate step before moving to reject.
_ _Active Security Threat*: Nomi Health is currently under an active email impersonation campaign with 5,000+ spoofed emails blocked (January 8-14, 2026)
_ _Security Best Practice*: Gradual DMARC rollout - quarantine first, then reject
_ _Leadership Approval*: Leadership and vSOC have been notified and support this change
_SEC Team Decision_: Implement 100% quarantine first as safer intermediate step, then move to reject after monitoring period.
* Quarantine sends failing emails to spam folder (recoverable)
* Quarantine allows monitoring for legitimate sender issues before full enforcement
_ _MX servers* - Mail servers in MX record

h1. Monitor DMARC reports for 48-72 hours
h1. Verify no legitimate email going to spam
h1. Create follow-up ticket for Phase 2 (reject)

* Recipients can recover legitimate emails from spam if needed
* Spoofed emails will be in spam (most users won't see them)

h1. Revert DMARC record to previous value:

Decision: Master/Minion Ingress Pattern Redesign,DEVOPS-7864,318516,Task,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,03/Dec/25 12:13 PM,29/Jan/26 10:37 AM,,29/Jan/26 10:37 AM,,,,,,0,planned,,,,,,,"h2. Objective
Determine the architectural approach for redesigning the master/minion Ingress pattern in Gateway API. This is a CRITICAL BLOCKER affecting 189 ingresses (92% of NGINX infrastructure).
* Master Ingress: Defines global server-level config (HSTS headers, redirects, security headers)
* Minion Ingresses: Attach to master via nginx.org/mergeable-ingress-type annotations
* Provides centralized configuration with per-namespace customization
* Problem: NO direct Gateway API equivalent exists
* Convert master and minions to separate HTTPRoutes
* Each HTTPRoute handles its own hostnames/paths
* Requires duplicating common filters across routes
* Cons: Less DRY, more maintenance burden
* Use HTTPRouteFilter policies for global config (HSTS, security headers, redirects)
* Create shared policies referenced by multiple HTTPRoutes
* Gateway API native approach aligned with design philosophy
* Status: Supported by BOTH NGINX Gateway Fabric and Envoy Gateway
* Pros: More maintainable, extensible, best practices
* Apply policies at namespace level for all routes
* Affects resource design and policy patterns for both controllers
* (/)/Decision applicable to both NGINX Gateway Fabric and Envoy Gateway

We encountered issues attempting to create a blue/green deployment for this upgrade:
_Problem:_ The GREEN instance consistently fails with {{invalid store}} errors.
This appears to be related to DDL (Data Definition Language) changes being executed on the {{use-dev-pgappdb1}} instance while the blue/green deployment is being created.

When RDS creates the green instance via logical replication, any concurrent DDL operations (such as {{ALTER TABLE}}, {{CREATE INDEX}}, {{DROP COLUMN}}, etc.) can cause replication to fail with ""invalid store"" errors because the schema changes cannot be replicated properly to the green instance.

Overview

The current GitHub Actions workflows for Zeus database operations use the {{jenkins}} MySQL user, which has overly broad permissions on production database servers. This violates the principle of least privilege and creates unnecessary security risks. This ticket covers the creation of properly scoped CI users and migration of workflows to use them.
# The {{jenkins}} user likely has excessive global privileges
# Same user credentials used across dev and prod database hosts
# No clear audit trail specific to CI/CD operations
# Potential for accidental or malicious abuse of permissions
Based on workflow analysis, the CI user needs these privileges on {{%_zeus}} and {{%_hive}} database patterns:

column3: Creating databases and tables during import
Reading data for mysqldump and queries

column1: * ❌ {{SUPER}} - Not needed for any workflow operation
h2. Proposed Solution: Dual CI User Strategy
h3. Create Two Separate CI Users
* *Scope:* Full permissions on dev databases only
h3. Benefits of Dual User Strategy
* ✅ Separation of dev and prod environments
* ✅ Reduced blast radius if credentials compromised
* ✅ Allows different permission models per environment
h3. Step 1: Create Development CI User
-- Create user for development database operations
GRANT CREATE USER, RELOAD, SHOW DATABASES ON *.* TO 'ci-github-actions-dev'@'%';
-- Grant database-level privileges on dev databases only
GRANT CREATE, DROP, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ALTER, INDEX,
GRANT CREATE, DROP, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ALTER, INDEX,
-- Grant GRANT OPTION for creating users with permissions

During further investigation of app-only credential viability across n8n workflows, we discovered that the original spike scope was incomplete. This finding affects the architecture decision significantly.
h3. The Discovery: Teams Trigger Cannot Use App-Only Credentials
We attempted to replace the delegated OAuth credential in the Microsoft Teams Trigger node with our app-only test credential (ms-graph-client-credentials-test).
Result: The app-only credential does not even appear in the credential dropdown - n8n filters it out automatically.
h3. Root Cause: Event Subscriptions Require Delegated Permissions Only
Investigation of Azure AD permissions revealed:
Conclusion: The Microsoft Graph Subscription.ReadWrite.All permission (required for event subscriptions) does not exist as an application permission. It only exists as a delegated permission.
This is by design - Microsoft restricts event subscriptions to authenticated users to maintain accountability and audit trails.
h3. This Limitation Extends Across Microsoft Services
The pattern is not specific to Teams:
h3. Scope of Impact on Original Goal
The original objective was: ""Enable unattended operation without requiring human re-authentication""
For the dev-eks-oncall-engineer-v2 workflow to function autonomously:
* Read channel messages (HTTP Request with app-only token)
* Reply to thread (403 Forbidden - Teamwork.Migrate.All unavailable)
Verdict: App-only migration is fundamentally not viable for this workflow because:
1. The trigger requires delegated auth (cannot be eliminated)
2. Write operations require delegated auth (cannot be eliminated)
3. This leaves only read operations viable for app-only - but the workflow needs write capability
h3. Revised Recommendation: Service Account Approach
Since app-only migration is not viable, the recommended alternative is a Service Account Approach:
## Create or designate a dedicated service account:
* OR a bot user account with delegated permissions
2. Grant this shared account delegated OAuth permissions:
3. Store a single OAuth token for the shared account in n8n credentials
4. All workflows use this shared credential
## Evaluate whether service account approach is acceptable for organizational requirements
2. If acceptable: Create follow-up spike for service account credential implementation
3. If not acceptable: Keep current delegated OAuth approach (status quo)
4. Document this finding as architectural constraint for future Microsoft 365 integrations in n8n

After comprehensive investigation, we are concluding this experiment as _not feasible_ with the originally envisioned app-only approach.
The app-only OAuth2 migration is fundamentally blocked by Microsoft's architectural design:
* Event subscriptions (triggers) require delegated permissions only
* Message sending operations require delegated permissions only
* These constraints apply universally across all Microsoft 365 services
* No application-only equivalent exists for these operations
h4. Recommended Path Forward: Bot Framework Approach
Rather than abandoning the goal of centralized credential management, we recommend pivoting to a _Bot Framework registration_ approach:
* Azure Bot Service provides native Teams integration and event handling
* Bots use a different authentication model that sidesteps the subscription limitation
* Provides webhook-based event delivery without requiring Graph API subscriptions
* Maintains the ability to handle triggers, reads, and writes from a single authenticated context
Create a new SPIKE ticket to evaluate:

We are undable to decrypt the files sent by the client Gilead, who is sending to mercer-workday. The PGP encryption key attached tot his ticket is what we are currently using, and as far as I know, it doesn’t have an expiration date, but would you confirm it. I’m attaching a picture of the relevant logs as well, which shows that the encryption worked but decryption failed.
Let me know if you need any other details.
The GPG decryption process was failing with the following error:
{code}gpg: WARNING: message was not integrity protected

The encrypted file was created without *Modification Detection Code (MDC)* integrity protection. Modern GPG versions (2.1+) refuse to decrypt files lacking MDC as a security measure to prevent tampering attacks.
Modified the {{gpgdecrypt}} script at {{use-prod-sftp1:/root/sftp_scripts/gpgdecrypt}} by adding the {{--ignore-mdc-error}} flag to line 22:
After applying the fix, decryption now works successfully:
gpg: WARNING: unsafe permissions on homedir '/mnt/creds/keys/.gnupg'
gpg: encrypted with 4096-bit RSA key, ID 9A15EDED3F6C6362, created 2016-01-06
gpg: WARNING: message was not integrity protected
The file now decrypts successfully. The warnings are informational and don't prevent decryption.

The {{--ignore-mdc-error}} flag allows processing of legacy encrypted files while maintaining security awareness through the warning message. This is the recommended approach for handling older encrypted files that lack integrity protection.","19/Aug/25 8:59 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;[~accountid:6080515c1417e2006ae082ea] Is it possible to ask the Vendor to provide files that include the MDC?
Here is a summary of what you can ask them:

{quote}We've identified that some of your encrypted files are missing integrity protection, which is causing processing delays. To ensure secure and reliable file processing, please update your encryption process.

When encrypting files for upload, please ensure Modification Detection Code (MDC) is enabled. This adds integrity protection to prevent tampering and ensures compatibility with modern security standards.
* Security: Protects against file tampering during transmission

column1: Create a custom Backstage plugin that automatically provides Software Catalog items from GitHub repositories containing {{ballista.yml}} files, integrating the Ballista deployment platform with Backstage's service catalog.
* *Strategy*: Create a custom {{CatalogProcessorParser}} instead of an {{EntityProvider}} to leverage Backstage's existing GitHub organization scanning capabilities
* *Rationale*: Avoid duplicating battle-tested logic for sifting through GitHub repositories
* *Implementation*: Extend Backstage's built-in YAML file processing located at {{/plugins/catalog-node/src/processing/parse.ts}}
* *Package Distribution*: Use Ballista to publish a Node package for easy distribution
* *Integration Method*: Custom processor approach rather than entity provider
* *File Processing*: Custom YAML file processing method to handle {{ballista.yml}} format
Backstage requires specific fields that aren't automatically available in {{ballista.yml}} files:
* *{{owner}}*: Must be automatically determined from ballista.yml or repository metadata
* *{{lifecycle}}*: Needs automatic determination logic (e.g., development, production, experimental)
Based on Backstage's documentation patterns, the solution needs:
* Converts Ballista service definitions to Backstage entities
* Maps Ballista metadata to Backstage required fields
* Automatically determine {{owner}} from repository metadata or configuration
* Assign appropriate {{lifecycle}} values based on service characteristics
* Generate proper Backstage entity metadata and specifications
* Develop logic to extract or infer {{owner}} and {{lifecycle}} from ballista.yml or repository context
* Handle cases where these fields cannot be automatically determined
* Ensure easy updates and version compatibility
* Bridge the gap between Ballista's deployment-focused YAML structure and Backstage's catalog entity format
* Handle multiple artifacts and services within a single ballista.yml file

A seamless integration where services with {{ballista.yml}} files automatically appear in the Backstage Software Catalog, providing developers with a unified view of all services regardless of their deployment platform configuration method.

column1: I've completed an analysis of the n8n webhook requirements and our current infrastructure. Here's a comprehensive summary focused on *external webhook implementation* (e.g., Datadog, GitHub, external monitoring systems):
* ✅ n8n Helm chart already includes webhook support templates ({{deployment.webhook.yaml}}, {{service.webhook.yaml}}, {{configmap.webhook.yaml}})

*Answer: YES* - For external services like Datadog, we need internet-facing ingress with proper security controls.
* Deploy dedicated webhook pods (already supported in templates)
* Use public ingress with NGINX ingress controller
* Implement rate limiting and IP whitelisting where possible
n8n supports multiple authentication methods. For external webhooks, I recommend:
* Use External Secrets Operator (already configured in n8n templates)
* *Header Auth* (Recommended): Custom header with secret token (e.g., {{X-Webhook-Token}})
* *Basic Auth*: Username/password (less flexible for external services)
* *JWT*: For advanced scenarios requiring token expiration
* *No Auth*: Never use for external webhooks

This implementation plan outlines the RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) configuration for n8n Enterprise to achieve:
* *DEV Environment*: Full read/write access for all users via ""Project Editor"" role
* *PROD Environment*: Read-only access for all users via ""Project Viewer"" role
* *Workflow Promotion*: GitHub Actions-based selective workflow deployment from DEV to PROD using service account with ""Project Admin"" role
*Solution*: Leverage n8n Enterprise's native RBAC features for clean, maintainable access control.
## *DEV Environment*: Users can create/update/delete workflows freely
2. *PROD Environment*: Absolute read-only - no changes via UI by anyone
3. *Workflow Execution*: PROD workflows must still be able to run/execute
4. *Workflow Deployment*: GitHub Actions for selective workflow promotion
5. *User Experience*: Users work entirely in n8n UI without Git knowledge
n8n Enterprise provides native role-based access control that perfectly meets our requirements:
* *Project Admin*: Full control over projects, workflows, and members
* *Project Editor*: Can create, update, and delete workflows (for DEV)
* *Project Viewer*: Read-only access to workflows, cannot execute manually (for PROD)
* *Native Solution*: Built-in support, no workarounds needed
* *Clean UI*: Edit buttons properly disabled for viewers
* *No Database Complexity*: Application handles permissions internally
* *Workflow Import Works*: Admin service account can import while users have read-only access
h2. How RBAC Works with Execution
With Project Viewer role in PROD:
* *Workflows CAN run* - Automated executions, schedules, and webhooks work
* *Manual execution DISABLED* - Viewers cannot manually trigger workflows
* *Workflows CAN'T be modified* - No creating, editing, or deleting workflows
* *Execution data IS saved* - For debugging and monitoring
* *Credentials ARE visible* - But cannot be modified
h3. Phase 1: Configure RBAC in n8n Enterprise
Since n8n Enterprise is already deployed with licensing in both environments:
* Create projects in both DEV and PROD to organize workflows
* Consider organizing by team, department, or function
* All users: ""Project Editor"" role (full read/write access)
* Service account: ""Project Admin"" role (for GitHub Actions imports)
* Generate API key and store as GitHub secret
* {{N8N_PROD_ADMIN_API_KEY}} - Service account API key for PROD
* Add the GitHub Actions workflow (see full implementation document)
* Note its ID from the URL
* Run GitHub Action with the workflow ID
## *Test as Regular User (Project Viewer) in PROD*:
* Execute manually → ✗ Not allowed for viewers
2. *Test as Service Account (Project Admin) via API*:
* Import workflow via API → ✓ Should work
* Create/edit workflows → ✓ Full access via API only
1. Accept comma-separated workflow IDs as input
2. Export workflows from DEV using API
3. Remove ID field to avoid conflicts (using jq)
4. Import to PROD using service account API
The GitHub Actions runner in DEV-EKS can reach PROD n8n via internal routing:
* *Routing*: Uses Route53 private hosted zones and AWS internal routing
* *No external exposure*: All traffic stays within AWS network
* *Clean user experience* with properly disabled UI elements

The implementation is straightforward and leverages n8n's built-in capabilities for a maintainable solution.",11/Jul/25 1:08 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;DEVOPS-7243 implements the GitHub Actions workflow needed for the n8n RBAC solution,"11/Jul/25 1:08 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Created implementation ticket for GitHub Actions workflow:

This ticket is to create a Technical Design Document (TDD) for implementing a web-based user interface for the Artemis Exchange system. The UI will replace the current manual Python script approach for managing Snowflake views, enabling Data Managers and CSMs to self-service view modifications without DevOps intervention.

The Artemis Exchange is a healthcare analytics data sharing platform that delivers cleaned, structured healthcare data to customers through automated Snowflake database shares. Currently, view management requires manual execution of Python scripts, which is error-prone and requires DevOps involvement.
1. Design a containerized web application for Exchange view management
2. Enable self-service operations for Data Managers and CSMs
3. Support all existing customer configurations (reader accounts and direct shares)
4. Integrate with existing Artemis-Auth service for authentication
5. Maintain audit trails for compliance requirements
6. Prepare for future Zeus automation integration
* Add, replace, or drop columns in customer views through intuitive UI
* Support for bulk operations across multiple customers
* Automatic detection of reader vs direct share configurations
* Complete audit logging with user identification
* Infrastructure: EKS, RDS PostgreSQL, AWS Secrets Manager
* Deployment: Containerized on existing Kubernetes clusters
6. Implementation plan with phases and tickets
* Design supports all current Exchange operations
* Authentication integrated with existing Artemis-Auth service

This will enable granular permissions for portal operators who manage AWS Transfer Family resources.
- Portal operators are Artemis-authenticated users who manage Transfer Family services
- Transfer Family users are the actual SFTP/FTPS users (separate from portal operators)
- Currently, all authenticated users have full admin access (flat permission model)
** artemis_user_id field (unique, linked to Artemis Auth 'sub' claim from JWT)
** Email address field (synchronized from Artemis Auth)
** Role field for permission levels (superadmin, admin, readonly)
** Proper indexes on email and artemis_user_id
* Implement auto-creation/update of admin user records:
** Create/update record on successful login via /api/v1/auth/login endpoint
** Update record on token validation for existing JWT-based auth
** Handle race conditions using database constraints
** Set default role as 'admin' for new users
- superadmin: Full access + manage other admin users
- admin: Full Transfer Family management (current default)
- readonly: View-only access to Transfer Family resources
** Create permission decorator/dependency for FastAPI routes
- Transfer Family write operations: admin or superadmin
- Transfer Family read operations: all authenticated users
** Add current user's role to API responses where relevant
** Work with new username/password login endpoint
** Handle 5-minute token expiration with refresh tokens
** Ensure both auth methods create/update admin user records
** Test with both auth methods (login endpoint and JWT validation)
- Use SQLAlchemy's unique constraints to prevent duplicate artemis_user_id
- Implement as FastAPI dependency for easy integration
- Add role to structlog context for audit logging
- Consider caching user roles in Redis with 5-minute TTL (matching token expiration)
1. Admin users table created with proper schema
2. Users auto-created on first authentication (both methods)
3. Role-based permissions enforced on all endpoints
4. Existing flat permission model continues to work during migration
5. Comprehensive test coverage for all scenarios

This details the process to create a container image for Backstage based on the POC work done in [DEVOPS-6681] and deploy it to our ECR repository. The Backstage instance will serve as an Internal Developer Portal (IDP) that will allow developers to create different compositions for Crossplane resources.
* Update the Dockerfile to ensure it includes all necessary plugins:
* Configure proper environment variable handling for secrets and configuration
### 2. Set up CI/CD Pipeline for Container Build
* Create a GitHub Action workflow that will:
* Run tests to verify the image works as expected
* Push the image to our ECR repository with proper versioning
* Tag images with both version numbers and 'latest' for easier deployment
* Set up proper repository in ECR with appropriate permissions
* Configure ECR lifecycle policies for image management
* Document the repository structure and access patterns
* Document the configuration options for the container
* Create runbooks for common operations and troubleshooting
* Provide examples of how to use the container in our environment
Copy package files and install dependencies
Copy the rest of the application
Use tini as entrypoint to handle signals properly
Create a `app-config.yaml` file that can be overridden with environment-specific values:
methods: [GET, HEAD, PATCH, POST, PUT, DELETE]
allow: [Component, System, API, Group, User, Resource, Location]
* IAM Permissions for GitHub Actions to push to ECR
* All secrets should be stored in AWS Secrets Manager or similar service
* Use IAM roles for service accounts when possible
* Implement proper RBAC for both Backstage and Kubernetes

* Set up network policies to restrict access between components",,Ari Sela (Artemis),,,,,,,,,,,,,61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,DEVOPS-6681,DEVOPS-7054,DEVOPS-7055,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,com.atlassian.servicedesk.plugins.approvals.internal.customfield.ApprovalsCFValue@24a90b7d,,,,,,Ari Sela,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,0.0,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,None,,,,,,,"{pullrequest={dataType=pullrequest, state=MERGED, stateCount=4}, json={""cachedValue"":{""errors"":[],""summary"":{""pullrequest"":{""overall"":{""count"":4,""lastUpdated"":""2025-07-11T09:12:16.000-0600"",""stateCount"":4,""state"":""MERGED"",""dataType"":""pullrequest"",""open"":false},""byInstanceType"":{""oAuth-com.xiplink.jira.git.jira_git_plugin"":{""count"":2,""name"":""Git Integration for Jira by GitKraken""},""GitIntegrationforJirabyGitKraken"":{""count"":2,""name"":""Git Integration for Jira by GitKraken""}}}}},""isStale"":true}}",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,1

Here's what you need to do to fix this:
Run pipenv lock in your local environment to regenerate the Pipfile.lock file with the new bleach dependency
Commit and push the updated Pipfile.lock file along with your Pipfile

# The Aella control service ({{aella_ctrl}}) is a Python service that appears to be responsible for monitoring and managing other Aella components.

# Looking at the service configuration, we see that {{aella_ctrl}} is running as Python 2 ({{/usr/bin/python2 /usr/sbin/aella_ctrl}}), which is quite outdated and might explain some of the file cleanup issues.

# The service is set up with specific resource limits (25% CPU quota, 500MB memory limit) that could potentially be causing issues if the cleanup routine is getting terminated due to resource constraints.{quote}

column10: *_10062_*:*_1_*:*_3983,,,"04/Mar/25 12:51 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;According to AWS's documentation on lifecycle transition considerations, there are specific limitations on which storage class transitions are allowed.

column1: *Key limitation*: We cannot use lifecycle policies to transition objects from Intelligent-Tiering to Standard-IA.
The allowed S3 lifecycle transitions follow a generally one-way progression:
* Standard → Standard-IA → Intelligent-Tiering/One Zone-IA → Glacier → Glacier Deep Archive
So once objects are in Intelligent-Tiering, our lifecycle options become more limited:
* We can transition them to Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive
* We cannot transition them back to Standard or to Standard-IA
This explains why our ""Transition to IA"" rule isn't working on the bulk of our data - those objects are already in Intelligent-Tiering and can't be moved to Standard-IA via lifecycle policies.
If we absolutely need objects in Standard-IA, the only way would be to:
# Copy them back to Standard storage class first (which costs money for the copy operation)
# Then let the lifecycle policy move them to Standard-IA
But this approach would likely be more expensive than just keeping them in Intelligent-Tiering, which already optimizes costs based on access patterns.

column1: Help Hardik write up documentation for RFP,DEVOPS-6561,164771,Task,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,High,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,25/Feb/25 8:04 AM,25/Feb/25 12:39 PM,,25/Feb/25 12:39 PM,,DevOps 5.4 - March 5th ,,,,0,interrupt,productrequest_notforecasted,,,,,,"[~accountid:6170476d16119e0069bb83e9]  was asking information related to our CI/CD pipeline and DR strategies, here are the answers I came up with for him:
What is your approach to high availability and disaster recovery (RPO, RTO, replication, failover)?

Our metadata is stored in AWS RDS with Multi-AZ configurations, ensuring synchronous replication and automatic failover within the same region. Daily automated snapshots (with 14 days’ retention) help ensure data can be recovered quickly.

Our application services run on a Kubernetes cluster deployed across multiple Availability Zones (AZs). This architecture leverages Kubernetes’ self-healing and auto-scaling features, allowing services to quickly recover or be re-scheduled if an AZ becomes unavailable.

We leverage Elastic Load Balancers to distribute incoming application traffic across multiple instances and AZs. This not only enhances performance but also ensures that if one instance or even an entire AZ becomes unavailable, traffic is automatically rerouted to healthy nodes, thereby supporting both HA and DR objectives.

We use Snowflake for our analytical data needs, which is deployed in US-EAST-1. Snowflake manages its own HA/DR strategy with built-in replication and failover processes, providing a robust guarantee of data availability as long as the region remains operational.
* _Service Assurance:_ Relying on Snowflake’s internal SLAs and procedures, we benefit from a high-availability model designed for enterprise needs.
Our caching layer is provided by ElastiCache clusters set up in Multi-AZ mode, ensuring that in-memory data remains available even if one AZ encounters an issue.
* _Failover:_ Automated and rapid, in line with AWS’s best practices.
What practices does your company have to prevent downtime in the case of a disaster?
Each component of our architecture—from the database and application layer to the caching layer—is deployed across multiple Availability Zones to ensure redundancy.

Leveraging AWS and Kubernetes’ automated failover capabilities means that if a failure occurs, services are restored quickly with minimal intervention. Daily backups for our RDS instances provide an additional layer of data protection.

We have robust monitoring and alerting in place to detect and respond to issues immediately. Regular DR testing and infrastructure reviews help ensure that our procedures remain effective and that recovery objectives are met.
Our deployment is fully managed through infrastructure as code, which enables us to rapidly replicate or redeploy services if needed.
What is the SLA associated to disaster recovery procedures?
* With our multi-AZ setup across AWS services and Snowflake’s managed HA/DR, we target a high-availability SLA of around 99.9%.
Based on documentation we created last year for RTO/RPO determinations: [https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/EN/pages/3091365966/Artemis+RTO+and+RPO+determination+and+strategies
* Our RPO can be up to 24 hours since we perform nightly RDS snapshots of the customer databases.

* In case we had to re-provision all our networking/computing resources (VPC, EKS, any additional resource used in AWS) is around 4 hours (being conservative in our estimation since we have migrated some resources to Kubernetes which can speed up our process a bit)
Here is our current Product Disaster Recovery Plan: [https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/AGKB/pages/50233783/Product+Disaster+Recovery+Plan
I don’t know where the SLA is since that was handled by Kathy from SEC for hitrust/SOC2 compliance reporting.
Are new releases backward-compatible with existing integrations or customizations?
*Are we talking about Data or API schemas?*
* *If we talk about data I don't think we are since I often have to prepare a restoration of a backed up Database in case we need to roll back.*
* *If it means API changes you would need to check with DEV teams.*
What rollback mechanisms or procedures exist if a release introduces critical issues?
* *Identify the Stable Commit:* When an issue is detected, pinpoint the last known good state in your Git repository.
* *Revert the Commit:* Use Git’s native capabilities (e.g., {{git revert}} or resetting to a previous commit) to roll back the code. This change is then pushed to the Git repository.
* *GitOps Sync:* Your GitOps tool (such as ArgoCD or Flux) detects the change and automatically syncs the EKS cluster to the previous stable state.

* *Deployment Rollback:* The GitOps tool will update your Kubernetes manifests (Deployments, Services, etc.) to match the reverted commit. This ensures the cluster is running the last stable configuration.
* *Automated Verification:* Implement health checks and observability tools to verify that the rollback has restored service stability.

* *Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR):* If your release issue involves data corruption or schema changes, you might need to restore your RDS instance to a previous time. AWS RDS supports point-in-time recovery, which can be used to revert the database to its state before the problematic release.
* *Snapshot-Based Restore:* Alternatively, if you have regular snapshots, you can restore from the latest snapshot taken before the release.

* *Coordinated Rollback:* Ensure that the restored database state is compatible with the rolled-back application code. This may require running database migrations or adjustments to align the schema with the earlier version of the application.
How do you manage code/configuration promotion from development to staging and production environments?
** Developers merge feature commits to the main branch.
** The GitOps operator (Argo CD) automatically deploys the updated configuration to DEV.
** We create a PR that copies the updated image tags (and any other promotion-worthy changes) from the DEV directory to the PREPROD environment.
** This PR is reviewed and approved by a lead/manager.
** Once approved and merged, the updated configuration is deployed to the PREPROD environment.
** Simultaneously, the QA team conducts regression/functional testing in PREPROD and automated tests run in a secondary environment.
** Following successful testing and a go/no-go meeting, another we prepare another PR that updates the production configuration with the changes tested in PREPROD.
** This PR is subject to approval solely by the DevOps team, ensuring that only changes that meet strict release criteria are deployed.
** Upon approval, the GitOps operator deploys the configuration changes to the production environment.
Do you maintain automated test suites (unit, integration, performance) to ensure platform stability during upgrades?

column1: Update zeus templates to use KEDA Autoscaling for MARA workers,DEVOPS-6489,163666,Story,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela,638f614ea593cb822e988133,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,05/Feb/25 10:17 AM,05/Feb/25 9:02 PM,,05/Feb/25 11:48 AM,,DevOps 5.2 - February 5th,,,,0,interrupt,planned,,,,,,"We need to make a change to our HPA for the workers to be optional through a new variable in the values file, this will allow us to manually disable HPA as we start migrating lower environments to use KEDA for autoscaling.
* Update the templates/mara/hpa.yaml to be optionally created based on new variable in values.yaml
** New value should be under the mara section and should be called keda_scaling_enabled
** It should default to true in case there is no value
** Update the hpa.yaml to create the file if not ecs_enabled OR keda_scaling_enabled
* Update the templates/mara/deployments.yaml to use the --cloudwatch argument if keda_scaling_enabled is set to true or if ecs_enabled
* Include the following resources to the templates for hcg:
* Verify this will work with following steps:
** Change the applicationSet branch to whatever you are using to deploy these changes
** Verify existing environments still have their hpa/deployment working as expected (without the new boolean flag of keda_scaling_enabled
** Verify Qa/ PREPROD are still using the ECS workers and run test data set to make sure HCG works as expected.
** Update one of the environments to use keda_scaling_enabled
** Verify that environment has its hpa removed and deployment updated to use --cloudwatch
** Run test data set to make sure workers scale up and down for HCG and document in this ticket
* Tested for lower environment + QA/PREPROD working as expected

* Changes merged to master",,,,,,,,,,,,,com.atlassian.servicedesk.plugins.approvals.internal.customfield.ApprovalsCFValue@1efd15e7,,,,,,Ari Sela,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,0.0,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,None,,,,,,,"{pullrequest={dataType=pullrequest, state=MERGED, stateCount=2}, json={""cachedValue"":{""errors"":[],""summary"":{""pullrequest"":{""overall"":{""count"":2,""lastUpdated"":""2025-02-05T11:44:53.000-0700"",""stateCount"":2,""state"":""MERGED"",""dataType"":""pullrequest"",""open"":false},""byInstanceType"":{""oAuth-com.xiplink.jira.git.jira_git_plugin"":{""count"":1,""name"":""Git Integration for Jira by GitKraken""},""GitIntegrationforJirabyGitKraken"":{""count"":1,""name"":""Git Integration for Jira by GitKraken""}}}}},""isStale"":true}}",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,1

Last month, I opened up a different helpdesk ticket [https://helpdesk.nomihealth.com/app/itdesk/ui/requests/148981000015184859/details
The last comment was about a ticket with devOps being opened. Was a ticket opened that I can track? If not I can open one. I just am not sure where this ended up.
We need an S3 bucket called medispan-incoming and a credential set that a vendor can use to deposit information into the bucket.
I then need a service account or something appropriate to access files saved to that bucket.
* Create S3  bucket policy to only allow uploads with encryption enabled (default aws kms key is fine)
* Create IAM service account for access to the S3 bucket
* Create IAM policy to grant read/write access to the s3 bucket:
* Attach the newly created IAM service account and [~accountid:63486fd2b380bb46a091a120]  to the group
* Create IAM AWS credentials and store in secrets manager under services/s3/medispan
* Provide [~accountid:63486fd2b380bb46a091a120]  the bucket location and the IAM credentials

This should all be done through Terraform.",,Ari Sela (Artemis),Cameron Shellum (Artemis),,,,,,,,,,,,61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,63486fd2b380bb46a091a120,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,APS-356,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,23/Jan/25 8:21 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20250123-152027.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/66037,23/Jan/25 8:21 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20250123-152102.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/66038,23/Jan/25 8:53 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20250123-155212.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/66041,23/Jan/25 8:53 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20250123-155245.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/66044,23/Jan/25 8:53 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20250123-155319.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/66042,23/Jan/25 8:53 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20250123-155346.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/66043,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,"* IAM Service account and its policy provisioned

column1: * The HCG inputs were a total of 69 from which 59 were finished successfully
* 10 of the HCG workers were left pending
After looking into the issue we found the root cause:
* The KEDA worker is scaling based on the work_available metric in cloudwatch
* When a worker starts it will remove 1 unit from work_available
* Keda controller detects that work_available was reduced by 1 and will terminate one of the pods running

Since the average time each worker takes can vary depending on the vendor dataset then in cases of small datasets the pods finish in time before KEDA terminates the pods but in HCG workers where the job takes longer than X amount of minutes then the pod will be terminated before the pod can finish.
Some possible work arounds for this:
* We can increase the stabilizationWindowSeconds to at least 1 hour to let the pods terminate after most of them finish their work
** The problem with this is that smaller datasets will now take 1 hour at least to finish where currently they can finish this step within 5 minutes
* We can make adjustments to the worker code to reduce the metric value of work_available once they finish
** This could still have issues if the KEDA scaler decides to terminate the wrong pod.
* We can try using a scaledJob which would provision a new job for each worker

** Currently testing this option.","04/Feb/25 2:04 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We made an adjustment to go from using HPA+Statefulsets to using Jobs (Using ScaledJobs from KEDA) and were able to run a test data set and verified the jobs started/finished successfully and deleting themselves once the job was finished.
Im currently running Boeing again to verify it behaves correctly with large datasets.

* Operational overhead, including CI/CD pipeline complexity and ongoing maintenance.
* Cost estimates and potential long-term savings or expenses for both approaches.
A Confluence document will be created to:
* Highlight pros and cons of AWS-native vs. container-based solutions.

column3: smart-link] ","28/Jan/25 6:46 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Documentation on this effort from AWS’s perspective: [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/apn/enhancing-availability-and-amazon-ec2-spot-utilization-of-databricks-workloads-on-aws/

column1: ** The article focuses on improving both _availability_ and _cost-effectiveness_ for Databricks workloads on AWS through the strategic use of EC2 Spot Instances.
** While Spot Instances offer significant cost savings, they come with the risk of interruption when capacity is no longer available or when the Spot price changes.
** Maintaining availability in multi-node Databricks clusters requires strategies to mitigate Spot interruptions.
*#* Combining different instance types, sizes, or families increases the pool of available Spot capacity, reducing the likelihood of interruptions.
*#* Implement an automated mechanism that checks Spot market capacity and replaces interrupted Spot Instances with either new Spot capacity or On-Demand Instances when needed.
*#* Databricks autoscaling can spin up additional On-Demand Instances if Spot Instances are not immediately available, reducing downtime while still maximizing cost savings.
** _Databricks Pools_ allow you to pre-warm clusters so jobs can start quickly.
** By judiciously using Spot capacity for these pre-warmed instances, you can drastically reduce idle capacity cost.

** The post outlines a reference architecture that uses multiple Spot instance pools, fallback to On-Demand Instances when necessary, and other AWS services (such as AWS Auto Scaling and AWS Spot Fleet) to handle Spot interruptions automatically.
** *Diverse Spot Options*: Select multiple instance types and sizes to improve Spot availability.
** *Monitoring and Alerts*: Track Spot interruptions, cluster usage, and job performance.
** *Fallback Strategy*: Always have a plan to fail over to On-Demand Instances to avoid job failures when Spot capacity is unavailable.
** By following these patterns, organizations running Databricks on AWS can maintain a _highly available_ analytics platform while _optimizing costs_ via Spot Instances.
** This approach helps ensure that critical workloads are minimally impacted by Spot interruptions and can continue running even under volatile capacity conditions.
* Use spot instances to use spare VM instances for a below-market rate
* Great for interactive ad hoc/shared clusters
* Can use them for production jobs without SLAs
* Not recommended for production jobs with tight SLAs
* Never use spot instances for the driver
We should consider starting with LOWER ENVIRONMENTS first to see how they perform.
Documentation on how to implement this: [https://www.databricks.com/blog/2016/10/25/running-apache-spark-clusters-with-spot-instances-in-databricks.html

Description

This spike task is to evaluate if we can refactor our existing workspaces in Terraform Cloud to use the new Stacks feature. Terraform Cloud Stacks is a powerful configuration layer that simplifies managing infrastructure modules at scale. Stacks provide a new way to organize infrastructure by splitting Terraform configurations into components and then deploying/managing those components across multiple environments.
Current challenges with our existing workspace approach:
* Lack of unified lifecycle management for related resources
* Complex coordination between workspaces using run triggers
* Difficulty in managing infrastructure at scale
Determine feasibility, benefits, and level of effort required to migrate our existing Terraform Cloud workspaces to the Stacks model.
# Research and understand Terraform Cloud Stacks:
** Review official HashiCorp documentation for Stacks
** Understand the differences between Stacks and traditional workspaces
** Document the key benefits and potential limitations
** Analyze our current workspace structure and identify potential components
** Draft a proposed Stacks architecture for our infrastructure
** Identify how our existing modules would map to Stack components
** Document how Stacks would handle cross-component dependencies
** Develop a small-scale proof of concept using Stacks
** Validate dependency handling and orchestration capabilities
** Estimate level of effort to migrate existing workspaces
** Identify potential risks and mitigation strategies
** Document any potential performance or scalability impacts
** Create a detailed Confluence page documenting findings
** Include architecture diagrams, component breakdown, and migration strategy
** Provide recommendations on whether to proceed with Stacks adoption
** Detailed analysis of Terraform Cloud Stacks and its benefits
** Proposed architecture showing how our infrastructure would map to Stacks
** Clear breakdown of components and deployments
** Estimated Level of Effort (LOE) for migration
** At least 2 components in a Stack
** Proper handling of dependencies between components
** Key benefits over our current workflow
** Compatibility with our existing CI/CD pipeline
** Impact on developer workflow and productivity
* Clear recommendation on whether to proceed with Stacks adoption, with justification
* [Deploy a Stack with HCP Terraform Tutorial
* This is a spike task, so the primary deliverable is knowledge and documentation rather than production code
* Consider the public beta status of Stacks and potential implications for production use

column9: *_10002_*:*_1_*:*_0,,,"21/Nov/24 7:08 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We identified an increase in proteus requests to unleash:

column1: Datadog excludes 99% of all unleash requests since it would make us reach our log limit within hours so the actual number of requests is this X 99.
We also noticed the DNS requests increasing in PROD-EKS:
This shows the DNS requests in our PROD-EKS cluster.
We then noticed unleash was trying to scale unsuccessfully:
We decided to change the HPA on unleash to do only 1 replica with increased requests/limits and that stabilized it (or so it seemed).
We then identified that this was overwhelming our coredns service in prod-eks:
This was causing connectivity issues with all our services in prod-eks:
Thinking that the bottleneck was CoreDNS we decided to increase its requests/limits as well and it stabilized coreDNS.

We thought that having datastaging run 2 metric-syncs at the same time was causing issues with load performance in proteus/unleash so [~accountid:5c992b27520ecd756a46dd9d]  killed the metric-syncs running and we saw improvement for a moment.
At 9:04pm MT we received a new alert from Pagerduty that proteus was generating a lot of logs, indicating issues: [https://nomihealth.pagerduty.com/incidents/Q1ELJVCN3F2KFN
We saw another increase in CPU usage for proteus at around that time:
Unleash was also showing a slow CPU increase in that timeframe as well:
DNS requests to unleash from proteus also increased at an alarming rate:
After some troubleshooting we identified that proteus was spinning up workers for pulling features at an abnormal rate:
We decided to rollback the proteus release in prod at 11:16pm MT and verified all numbers started going down:
Proteus CPU usage compared to last week:
Unleash CPU compared to last week:

#* Choose *Symmetric* for the key type (as it supports encryption and decryption).
#* Enter a *description* for the key to make it easily identifiable.
#* Set the *region* to *the same region as your RDS snapshot* (where it is currently located).
#* Specify which IAM users or roles can *administer* the key (e.g., create grants, modify the policy).
#* Usually, you can assign your *admin role* here.
#* Define *IAM users and roles* that can use the key to encrypt and decrypt data.
#* Ensure your account’s IAM user or role has *usage permissions*.
#* You will need to add permission for the *us-west-2 account* to use the key. You can do this in the *key policy*:
#* After configuring other settings, you’ll reach the *Key Policy* section.
#* Add a new statement in the *key policy* that allows the *target account* to use the key:
#* Replace {{""TARGET_ACCOUNT_ID""}} with the *Account ID* of the destination account.
#* Review all configurations and click on *Create Key*.
h3. Step 2: Copy the RDS Snapshot with the New KMS Key
#* Go to the *Amazon RDS Console* and select *Snapshots* from the sidebar.
#* Choose the *encrypted snapshot* you want to copy.
#** *Destination Region*: Select the *region* where you want to copy the snapshot (e.g., {{us-west-2}}).
#** *New DB Snapshot Identifier*: Provide a unique name for the copied snapshot.
#*** Choose the *new KMS key* that you created earlier.
#* Click *Copy Snapshot* to initiate the copying process.
#* Wait for the snapshot copy to complete. This might take some time depending on the size of the snapshot.
h3. Step 3: Share the Copied Snapshot with Another Account
#* Once the snapshot copy is complete, select the newly copied *manual snapshot*.
#* Enter the *Account ID* of the target AWS account (the {{us-west-2}} account).
h3. Step 4: Access the Snapshot in the Target Account
# *Log in to the Destination AWS Account*:
#* Log in to the *target AWS account* in *us-west-2*.
#* Choose the *""Shared with me""* filter to view snapshots shared by other accounts.
#* If you want to make a copy of the shared snapshot in the *target account*, select it and click *Actions* > *Copy Snapshot*.
#* During the copy process, you can select a *new KMS key* from the target account if needed.
# *Create a New KMS Key* in the source account and share it with the target account by editing the key policy.
# *Copy the RDS Snapshot* using the new KMS key.
# *Share the Copied Snapshot* with the destination AWS account.
# *Access and Copy* the shared snapshot in the destination account for further use.

This process ensures your snapshot is encrypted with a key that can be shared securely, allowing the target account to decrypt and use the data. Let me know if you need more guidance on any of these steps!","04/Oct/24 1:28 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Snapshots being deployed.

Implement Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) queue using Terraform to handle notifications from our newly provisioned Amazon S3 bucket. These notifications will be triggered when files are delivered to the S3 bucket via AWS Transfer Family. The SQS queue will facilitate communication with our EC2 instance, enabling it to automatically initiate processing workflows upon file delivery. This setup aims to enhance the scalability, reliability, and automation of our file processing pipeline.
* *Infrastructure Automation:* Utilize Terraform to define and deploy SQS queues.
* *S3 Integration:* Configure the S3 bucket to send event notifications to the SQS queue upon successful file uploads.
* *Security:* Ensure proper permissions and policies are in place to allow S3 to communicate with SQS securely.
* *Processing Workflow:* Enable EC2 instances to listen to SQS queues and trigger necessary processing tasks when notifications are received.

* *Documentation & Testing:* Provide comprehensive documentation and validate the entire workflow through testing.",,Ari Sela (Artemis),Automation for Jira,Dillon Essley (Artemis),,,,,,,,,,,61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,557058:f58131cb-b67d-43c7-b30d-6b58d40bd077,61c37edef3037f006959ac69,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,13/Dec/24 7:41 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20241213-144102.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/64992,13/Dec/24 8:02 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20241213-144715.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/64993,13/Dec/24 8:06 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20241213-150451.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/64995,13/Dec/24 8:06 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20241213-150558.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/64994,13/Dec/24 8:45 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20241213-154403.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/64998,13/Dec/24 8:45 AM;ug:67c6ac61-c390-44a9-b9f4-f4ba31bb0802;image-20241213-154459.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/64997,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,"* *SQS Queues Provisioned via IaC:*

column1: ** {noformat}# iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -p udp -o enp0s8 –sport 1194 -j SNAT –to-source 192.168.2.254:32768-60999{noformat}

In essence, this command is setting up Source NAT for OpenVPN traffic. It's taking UDP packets coming from port 1194 (OpenVPN) and going out through the {{enp0s8}} interface, then changing their source IP to 192.168.2.254 and their source port to a port in the range 32768-60999.
This is typically used in scenarios where you want to:
# Hide the original source IP of the OpenVPN clients.
# Ensure replies can be routed back correctly.
# Potentially work around firewall restrictions by using a wide range of high ports.
Keep in mind that this kind of NAT can affect the ability to establish direct peer-to-peer connections between VPN clients, as it masks their original IP addresses.

The potential issue we see is when a PR is being merged to a branch other than the master/main branch. An example of this can be found in the ballista.yml on the triton repository here: [https://github.com/artemishealth/triton/blob/e42b43e06557953b4fe47da7b801d2866e8e0ce6/ballista.yml#L1C56-L1C109

column13: *_10062_*:*_1_*:*_25477745593,,,"14/Feb/25 6:53 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We updated our DEVOPS environment in DEV-EKS to support up to 100 HCG workers and ran a Home Depo refresh which uses 312 HCG subsets: [https://zeus-devops.internal.artemishealth.com/customers/058b4a31-4130-4ee8-bee1-e2d6986487ed/refreshes/fef7f91c-39cf-41cd-a54c-27ecb54fbe96

column1: We monitored the HCG worker metrics:
* The total amount of time it took HCG workers to finish was 8 1/2 hours
* The amount it takes ECS to finish this process is 2 hours and 10 minutes.
After analyzing the work of a single worker doing a single subset we found the following:
It took around 50 minutes for the worker to process a file where it would take the ECS worker ","14/Feb/25 7:31 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We identified 3 issues with the previous Refresh:
We detected multiple OOM containers during the refresh for home depot related to the workers
This caused subsets to not be finished, they would be interrupted and a new job would have to pick up the subset which would take an additional 45 minutes to do
It turns out that our workers were being terminated due to the EC2 instances being terminated due to CPU limitations, we can see this in this chart:
We kept seeing pods being evicted due nodes being terminated when CPU spikes would go up

An additional bottleneck we found is that the more workers you have in a single EC2 instance (node) the less bandwidth they will have to download the HCG input file, for smaller datasets this is not a problem but for larger ones that have files 60GB or bigger it starts causing lag issues.
On average we are seeing a throughput of 67MB/s which means that each worker takes around 20-25 minutes just to download the file.

This is an existing bottleneck in ECS as well, I will be creating a separate DEVOPS ticket to look into minimizing the number of subsets so it has to download less files due to having less workers","14/Feb/25 11:13 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We made the following adjustments in the DEVOPS environment to the worker request/limits:
This would have the following effects:
* Reduce the number of workers per EC2 node
* Increase the minimum memory per worker to make sure they wouldn't run out of it
We then ran a new refresh in the DEVOPS environment for the home depot:
Here are the results of the subsets:
Results of the logs showing start/complete subset processing:
Here is the summary of the events:
#* Average processing time: 40 minutes per worker
#* second wave of 100 workers completed in 40 minutes
#* third wave of 100 workers complete in 40 minutes
#* last 12 workers took around 4 hours (we are looking into this)
# The memory/CPU adjustments appear to have helped as the majority (97.1%) of subsets completed within a reasonable timeframe (under 135 minutes)
# There are still a few outliers that took significantly longer
# The process shows good parallelization with three main completion waves

I’ll bee looking into fixing the issue with the stragglers to see if we can reduce the number of hours per refresh to what prduction handles.","14/Feb/25 12:53 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We compared the costs of running the Home Depot refresh in PROD vs DEVOPS environment using EKS workers:
Total cost = 70 dlls for 1 refresh running for 3 hours (2 hours with 100 workers)
Assuming the SPOT instances ran in the following manner:
* 100 workers running for 2 hours and 20 minutes
The cost per minute for SPOT instance is .12 cents
Total cost: 28 dlls + 1.2 dlls + .36 cents = 30 dlls
We ended up saving 57% of comuting costs.","17/Feb/25 5:59 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;[~accountid:6086de7c5797db006964c7fe]  will be making the following adjustments to run a new refresh:
* Change the hcg-compute node pool to c4.8xlarge (they use 36 CPUs and 60GB of memory).
** This would theoretically allow us to run 5-6 workers per instance at a cost of $0.47 per hour compared to $0.12 per hour for 1 worker on an m5.2xlarge.
** In my opinion, we’d need to have at least 20 nodes running to support 100 workers, which would cost around $35 for 3 hours.
** It would also allow us to keep the nodes in Datadog to have their logs and metrics (otherwise we’d have to find a way to exclude them from Datadog).
* Change the max_workers back to 100; 200 didn’t work because it couldn’t schedule more than 120.
** {{command: [""/bin/sh"", ""-c"", ""sleep 3600""]}} (also give the pre-stop hook one hour for the container to finish)
* Manually test by launching 100 work_Available to verify that Karpenter spawns at least 5 pods per instance.

* Run the Home Depot refresh again to see how it behaves.",17/Feb/25 6:05 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;[~accountid:6086de7c5797db006964c7fe]  Im moving it to the next sprint so we can continue work on this,"19/Feb/25 7:55 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We have successfully tested running a Home Depot refresh in the DEVOPS environment that matches the HCG worker performance of production, details below:
* HCG workers took 2 hours and 25 minutes
Worker logs showing completion of subsets
* The issue we were seeing where the KEDA controller was removing workers before we could finish the last 12 subsets seems to have been fixed with increasing the worker life to 1 hour
* We set up 100 workers as a maximum for this test to replicate PROD conditions
* 100 workers used 12 nodes on average to process (c6i.16xlarge)
* 0.8494 cents per hour on SPOT: 10.20 per hour X 3 = 30.60 for full refresh
This was an overall success, we found the following adjustment we can make to improve performance:
* If we decided to increase max_workers to 312 this would take 33 nodes which would finish the HCG process in 35 minutes with a cost of: 16 dlls.
* We will be testing this change in devops environment

column1: Our workaround for now is setting the infrastructure node group min/desired/max node size to 10 to keep it from spinning up/down nodes.

column1: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: Unencrypted Origin Trusted (VSID-008) – Low,DEVOPS-6159,140240,Task,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Kathy McNaughton,61d75f9aa54af900698dae5a,Kathy McNaughton,61d75f9aa54af900698dae5a,29/Feb/24 1:55 PM,16/Nov/24 9:38 AM,,16/Nov/24 9:38 AM,,DevSecOps 4.42 - November 23rd,,,,0,found_work,interrupt,planned,,,,,"Description

An HTML5 cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) policy controls whether and how content running on other domains can perform two-way interaction with the domain that publishes the policy. The policy is fine-grained and can apply access controls per-request based on the URL and other features of the request.

If a site allows interaction from an origin that uses unencrypted HTTP communications, then it is vulnerable to an attacker who is in a position to view and modify a user's unencrypted network traffic. The attacker can control the responses from unencrypted origins, thereby injecting content that is able to interact with the application that publishes the policy. This means that the application is effectively extending trust to all such attackers, thereby undoing much of the benefit of using HTTPS communications.
Only trust origins that use encrypted HTTPS communications.

A good strategy is to look for an instance type in the newer generation that offers a balance between increased compute and memory resources. The m5 or m6g families might be suitable candidates because they provide improved performance and efficiency over the m4 family. For handling 300 connections with similar average and peak CPU utilization as you're currently experiencing, consider the following aspects:

* *CPU and Memory*: More connections mean more active processes and threads, which require both CPU and memory resources. A higher number of CPUs would help in maintaining low CPU utilization, while more memory would support the increased workload and connection overhead.
* *Network Performance*: Ensure that the instance type you choose has adequate network performance to handle the increased data throughput.

Given these considerations, you might consider an instance like m5.xlarge or m5.2xlarge for a balance of CPU, memory, and network performance. These instances offer more vCPUs and memory compared to m4.large, which should help in maintaining similar CPU usage levels even with the increased number of connections.
If we change from db.m4.large to an m5.2xlarge to increase our CPU and Memory by 4X.
The costs will increase by 4X as well to an average of 16.80dlls per day = 117 dlls per week

* The metrics table has something in it that's making it super shitty to query against, so recreating metric caches is taking longer than it should, causing 504 timeouts for users that are waiting for the cache rebuild
* We're rebuilding Nx (once per hermes container that services a chartdata request where a cache does not exist yet, even if it is in progress rebuilding

* Something appears to be clearing out the metric cache and triggering more rebuilds during the day - we do not know if this is customers changing metrics, something unexpected in the code causing it, or just correlation with the known problems above.
* Hotfix to only rebuild the cache once instead of N times concurrently where N is the number of hermes pods that have received a chartdata request with a non-existent cache
* Adding logging to more clearly identify the issue and understand the behavior
* Changes will raise an error if we're waiting longer than x seconds for the metrics cache / formula cache to rebuild
* Identify why the query for creating the cache sucks so much starting today

column15: *_10002_*:*_1_*:*_0,,,"10/Jan/24 5:09 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;After some troubleshooting we found a correlation between our HCG Workers that were in Kubernetes and the costs with the increase in traffic in our NAT Gateways:

column1: We then noticed that this issue stopped after we migrated the HCG workers from EKS to ECS (Zeus Hybrid) and noticed that for some reason our NAT EC2 instance in the PROD VPC wasnt picking up that outbound traffic:
We decided to try and do a reachability analyzer between our use-devcody-hcg1  EC2 instance and the S3 endpoint for HCG output (using the IP address wee got from traceroute 54.231.162.161)
We noticed that the Route table for the production VPC had a route being used to bypass the use-prod-router1 EC2 instance:
We saw that the Private production route table had an entry for PL-63a5400a which then showed us that we were routing all S3 traffic through a VPC endpoint configured by snowflake:
We concluded that the HCG workers in ECS were basically all routing traffic to S3 through this VPC endpoint which is why we couldnt identify any traffic from the use-prod-router1 NAT instance.

We then decided to test if adding the same logic to our DEV-EKS private subnets would fix the issue, so we started by testing the reachability from an EC2 node inside the private subnet of DEV-EKS to the S3 endpoint through the IP address:
After we made the following changes we re-tested:
Set up a new VPC Endpoint for the S3 AWS Service and associated to the private subnets of dev-eks.

We can verify that we are now routing S3 traffic directly through the VPC endpoint (within AWS) so we wont have the issue with the NAT gateways anymore.","10/Jan/24 5:10 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Todo:
* Bring in the changes through Terraform
* Create vpc endpoint for test-eks and associate it to private subnets for test-eks

* Create vpc endpoitn for prod-eks and associate it to private subnets for prod-eks (During maintenance window)",10/Jan/24 5:24 PM;5c992b27520ecd756a46dd9d;More todo: separate ticket to test and reevaluate the firewall around NAT since we may be significantly lowering the number of evaluations,"11/Jan/24 11:34 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;[~accountid:5c992b27520ecd756a46dd9d]  [https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/browse/DEVOPS-4932

column1: Will check.","14/Nov/23 2:28 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We found the root cause, it seems that as part of our cleanup of the Jenkins workers we are removing docker images that have not been used in a certain period of time and these Ballista jobs are trying to pull these images from nexus, the issue is that the Ballista jobs are not authenticating with nexus which generated that “no basic auth credentials” error.

It shows each of the application yamls that it finds in the apps/test-cluster path.
Each of these applications are then deployed in Argo with the namespaces defined in the application.yamls

Your current config has FluentD send directly to us.  Either way works, but it would be up to you to determine what is more efficient for you to use.  Sometimes it’s better to have the shipper send directly to us if you want to individually control shipping tokens.
We would need to work on the config file.  The instructions on the referenced page are using the plugin.  It would work but there are a couple of ways we could set things up.

I think option 3 might be the least amount of work.  You could filter out huge log files at the container level, stopping FluentD from crashing.  It should also let you test out fluentbit without making huge changes to your cluster.  I’m pretty sure your current FluentD would be able to receive the input from Fluentbit without any changes.
Let me know if this makes sense.

column8: *_10062_*:*_1_*:*_151062791,,,"20/Jul/23 9:15 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We found the root cause for missing artemis application logs as well as zeus logs:

{noformat}WHEN (log type is agent-k8s) AND (""logzio-signature"" is ""-947639980"") - hermes and artemos-app logs

We disabled these filters and added new ones to remove some unnecessary logging and we were able to get logs again for all our hermes environments:

column1: {noformat}-- Creating DB and Schema for cost-monitoring effort
-- Creating warehouse for testing cost-saving efforts.
-- View to get every single query that has been run in our database for the last year
-- Helpful to ask questions about how to do cost-saving.
-- View to get every single query that has been run in our database for the last year
-- Helpful to ask questions about how to do cost-saving.
select query_id, warehouse_name, database_name, schema_name, start_time, end_time, execution_time, compilation_time, total_elapsed_time, query_text
-- View to get every single query that has been run in our database for the last year
-- Helpful to ask questions about how to do cost-saving.
select database_name, schema_name, execution_status, avg(total_elapsed_time), min(total_elapsed_time), max(total_elapsed_time), count(*)
select database_name, schema_name, avg(total_elapsed_time), min(total_elapsed_time), max(total_elapsed_time), count(*)
create table admin_db.admin_db_monitoring.query_snapshot as select * from snowflake.account_usage.query_history;
-- Create separate table for the metering_history specifically.
(select start_time, end_time, entity_id as warehouse_id, name as warehouse_name, credits_used,
-- To see which queries are dominating our history table.
select query_type, count(1) as num_qs from admin_db.admin_db_monitoring.query_snapshot group by query_type order by num_qs desc;
--SELECT is the one where we try to lower down
--First thing we can focus on is CREATE_TABLE_AS_SELECT
-- Info on the type of queries, which warehouse it was executed in and how long it took
-- Take this back to PRODUCt/ENG team to tell them which queries are taking longer
--BASE_COST_WITHOUT_MULTIPLIER is X4 to get the actual cost per year per query type
-- DIVE into query history to see which query took over 20,126 seconds to complete in SELECT
-- Extreme case where this happened for query that took 300 minutes
-- Gives us percentiles of queries of median_times, basically distribution of query times.
select warehouse_name, any_value(pct_5)pct_5, any_value(pct_25)pct_25, median(total_elapsed_seconds) pct_50, any_value(pct_75) pct_75, any_value(pct_95) pct_95,
percentile_cont(0.05) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_5,
percentile_cont(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_25,
percentile_cont(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_75,
percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_95,
percentile_cont(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_99,
percentile_cont(0.995) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_99_5,
from (select warehouse_name,total_elapsed_time/1000 total_elapsed_seconds from admin_db.admin_db_monitoring.query_snapshot where total_elapsed_time is not null ))
order by pct_99_5 desc, pct_99 desc,pct_95 desc, pct_75 desc, pct_50 desc, pct_25 desc, pct_5 desc;
-- We can see STANDARD has 84,000,000 million queries where the 99% of them have an average of 2.29 seconds
-- We might want to have the PCT_99 running on a smaller warehouse. (This could impact total performance if we switch from 2 to 4 seconds)
-- possible to change suspend_time to 60 seconds.
