column1: Investigate cost saving measure for our snowflake account,DEVOPS-4247,121322,Task,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,05/Jul/23 1:36 PM,11/Oct/24 2:12 PM,,10/Jul/23 1:39 PM,,,,,,0,planned,,,,,,,"We had a meeting with the Nomi snowflake folks and saw that there might be some potential cost saving changes we could do to our Artemis account that would in theory not impact our performance.
* Changing warehouses to a smaller one
* Changing our suspend timeout from 900 seconds to 60 seconds (This is what nomi uses)
To verify these change would not have an impact we would like to do some analysis on how much of our warehouse are we actually using on a daily bases to see if we can change the warehouse type.

If we find that we could do some cost saving from the 2 items listed above as part of our analysis we can proceed to create implementation tickets for each of them and include some testing in lower environments to make sure we dont impact production performance.

We are working with [~accountid:5f64c98eaba96600713a09b8] on this one to make sure we use the same metrics Nomi is using to measure usage of our warehouse.",,Ari Sela (Artemis),,,,,,,,,,,,,61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,DEVOPS-4268,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,"Analysis done to measure usage of warehouse.
h3. Creating DB and Schema for cost-monitoring effort
h3. Creating warehouse for testing cost-saving efforts
h3. Create snapshot of table for faster results
h3. Create separate table for the metering_history specifically
(select start_time, end_time, entity_id as warehouse_id, name as warehouse_name, credits_used,
h3. See which queries are dominating our history table
{noformat}select query_type, count(1) as num_qs from admin_db.admin_db_monitoring.query_snapshot group by query_type order by num_qs desc;{noformat}
* ROLLBACK isnt such a big deal
* SELECT is the one where we try to lower down
* First thing we can focus on is CREATE_TABLE_AS_SELECT
h3. Info on the type of queries, which warehouse it was executed in and how long it took
* BASE_COST_WITHOUT_MULTIPLIER is X4 to get the actual cost per year per query type
* SELECT is costing us 40,000~ a year
* DIVE into query history to see which query took over 20,126 seconds to complete in SELECT
h3. Gives us percentiles of queries of median_times, basically distribution of query times.
{noformat}select warehouse_name, any_value(pct_5)pct_5, any_value(pct_25)pct_25, median(total_elapsed_seconds) pct_50, any_value(pct_75) pct_75, any_value(pct_95) pct_95,
percentile_cont(0.05) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_5,
percentile_cont(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_25,
percentile_cont(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_75,
percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_95,
percentile_cont(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_99,
percentile_cont(0.995) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_elapsed_seconds) over (partition by warehouse_name ) pct_99_5,
from (select warehouse_name,total_elapsed_time/1000 total_elapsed_seconds from admin_db.admin_db_monitoring.query_snapshot where total_elapsed_time is not null ))
order by pct_99_5 desc, pct_99 desc,pct_95 desc, pct_75 desc, pct_50 desc, pct_25 desc, pct_5 desc;{noformat}
* We can see STANDARD has 84,000,000 million queries where the 99% of them have an average of 2.29 seconds
* We might want to have the PCT_99 running on a smaller warehouse. (This could impact total performance if we switch from 2 to 4 seconds)
As discussed with [~accountid:5f64c98eaba96600713a09b8] we will be creating an implementation ticket with the following tasks:
* Configure our Datastaging environment and have it running for 2 weeks so we can compare the queries above between our standard warehouse vs cost_saving warehouse

* Monitor performance of datastaging with the cost_saving wharehouse which also includes the suspend_time change of 15 minutes to 60 seconds.",10/Jul/23 1:39 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Implementation ticket created and linked to this investigation.,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,121566,DEVOPS-4271,Cost-Saving features for Snowflake,Done,10/Jul/23 1:39 PM

# The file had to be written as a *single* coalesced file. When databricks writes files, it can only write them in a partitioned format - with hidden metadata within the .csv filename directory. So I used a *zeus* util method to clean out all of the parititioned non-csv files recusrively from that created directory (after the file is written) so only the single *csv* remains and the file movement process then moves 1 file instead of throwing errors when trying to move an entire directory. The move operation must be atomic!
# *Access denied* exceptions were thrown when I attempted to use the [*dbuils.fs.*
column3: http://dbuils.fs.mv]*cp* (_move_ and _copy_) methods to transfer the files form databricks to s3. However when I used the [*dbuils.fs.*
column4: http://dbuils.fs.mv]*put* method, the transfer finally worked. Very silly, Python is able to use its own internal libraries like shutil and os while Scala and Java cannot because apparently they do not perform a “*Put*”.

column1: Load testing on EKS Nodes for TEST-EKS,DEVOPS-4047,116308,Task,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,21/Apr/23 7:37 AM,10/May/23 2:24 PM,,26/Apr/23 8:19 AM,,,,,,0,interrupt,,,,,,,"On {{2023-04-20}} we deployed 3 artemis-app environments at the same time to our DEV-EKS cluster which had 3 applications running and this brought down the nodes and caused our cluster to crash (not respond and keep ejecting pods)
The existing configuration for DEV-EKS was:
* 3 Nodes of instance type t3.xlarge (16 GB x 4 Cores)
We found that the pods for hermes were causing memory/cpu OOM errors and this was due to the fact that at startup the pods consume up to 4GB of memory each and even the CPU usage spikes.
We were able to fix the issue by taking the following actions:
* Increasing node # to 12 with a max of 30
* Changing node types to t3a.2xlarge (32 GB X 8 CPU Cores)
* Slowly rolling out environments to avoid overwhelming the Nodes

We need to do load testing on our TEST-EKS cluster to see if with the updated configuration of nodes there is any issue. For this test we will need to update our Node gorup in TEST-EKS with the following changes:
* Increase node # to 12 with a max of 30
* Change node type to t3.2xlarge (32 GB X 8 CPU)
* Deploy 5 artemis-app environments (with existing deployment/hpa configuration) at the same time
* Deploy 3 artemis-app environments with updated deployment/hpa configuration of 10 hermes pods
We will need to capture screens of our node’s performance and verify that all the applications are stable after a few minutes to make sure pods are not being evicted.
* Increase node # to 15 with a max of 30
* Change node types in production to t3.2xlarge

* Deploy 5 artemis-app environments with existing configuration",,Ari Sela column13: *_10062_*:*_1_*:*_2524049473,,,"24/Oct/23 8:06 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;I have fully implemented the Argo Image updater in the deployments repository with the following applications:

column1: This is an application which automatically logs in to our ECR repository and generates json file used by Argo Image Updater to retrieve tags/images.
This is the Argo application that will detect any Application YAML that contains the image updater annotations and will try to detect any new tags and update the deployment yamls as needed.
An example of the annotations we created in the artemis-test application.yaml (CRD used by Argo CD) are listed below:
* image-list: This annotations tells Image Updater which images it should manage and it adds an alias so we can reference them in other annotations in short form
* pull-secret: This tells Image Updater where the ECR json that contains the auth information is located for that specific image (using the alias)

column1: Add External DNS service to our EKS clusters,DEVOPS-3938,106415,Story,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,20/Mar/23 6:50 AM,30/Mar/23 8:58 AM,,30/Mar/23 8:58 AM,,,,,,0,interrupt,,,,,,,"We need to implement the External DNS service into all our EKS clusters so we can provsion route53 records automatically whenever a new ingress is deployed (this will allow developers to test their environments without requiring help from DevSecOps)
Steps to do this (Tested in test-eks) below:
*Step 1: Add the following policy to AWS:*
*Step 2: Attach the policy to our existing Node Group role*
Step 3: Deploy the external deployment yaml:
{noformat}# comment out sa if it was previously created
namespace: externaldns # change to desired namespace: externaldns, kube-addons
- --domain-filter=k8s.artemishealth.com # will make ExternalDNS see only the hosted zones matching provided domain, omit to process all available hosted zones
- --policy=upsert-only # would prevent ExternalDNS from deleting any records, omit to enable full synchronization
- --aws-zone-type=private # only look at public hosted zones (valid values are public, private or no value for both)
Verify in pod logs that its working as expected by updating an existing ingress with the [metadata.annotations.external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname
column2: http://metadata.annotations.external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname]: “host” and make sure it deploys a route53 record in k8s.artemishealth.com

Increase size of nginx client_max_body_size in load balancer,DEVOPS-3557,98617,Task,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,High,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Kristopher Steinort,5d6402ff388d780dac23e5f2,Kristopher Steinort,5d6402ff388d780dac23e5f2,16/Dec/22 1:02 PM,05/Jan/23 9:08 AM,,05/Jan/23 9:08 AM,,,,,,0,interrupt,zeus,,,,,,"Currently, we’re running into a problem with a particular zeus endpoint, {{initiate-refresh-from-manifest}}.  The problem is, is that since our larger brokers have been expanding, so is their manifest. This is now so big, that it is running into our client_max_body_size limit on the LB. For example when attempting to start a large refresh:

On zeus-web we have this set {{client_max_body_size}} to 0 to allow everything. Currently, client_max_body_size is set to 75mb in our nginx config on the load balancer and that’s what is returning this error. From the LB nginx logs from above to prove this:

My ask is that we either bump this up on the load balancer or set it to 0 so that we don’t return an error code for users as these manifests get bigger as this will soon prevent refreshes from happening on our bigger broker clients. Happy to discuss alternatives as well.

For context the last deployed MMA refresh in prod has a manifest that is 70.5mb.",,Ari Sela (Artemis),Chris Hayes (Artemis),Jeff Shutt (Artemis),Kristopher Steinort,,,,,,,,,,61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,5af9a966d17d8405fa4348ed,557058:9f3a44d6-ce0c-4eb2-b1e9-747ebe31eb0a,5d6402ff388d780dac23e5f2,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,ZEUS-3822,,,,,,,,,,,,,,16/Dec/22 1:02 PM;rk:e10ab913-e054-4f89-b8c0-57bc6d8162db;image-20221216-195217.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/36077,16/Dec/22 1:02 PM;rk:e10ab913-e054-4f89-b8c0-57bc6d8162db;image-20221216-200052.png;https://artemishealth.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/attachment/content/36076,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,com.atlassian.servicedesk.plugins.approvals.internal.customfield.ApprovalsCFValue@4d06ba6c,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,0.0,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,None,,,,,,,"{pullrequest={dataType=pullrequest, state=MERGED, stateCount=4}, json={""cachedValue"":{""errors"":[],""summary"":{""pullrequest"":{""overall"":{""count"":4,""lastUpdated"":""2023-01-04T15:45:44.000-0700"",""stateCount"":4,""state"":""MERGED"",""dataType"":""pullrequest"",""open"":false},""byInstanceType"":{""oAuth-com.xiplink.jira.git.jira_git_plugin"":{""count"":2,""name"":""Git Integration for Jira by GitKraken""},""GitIntegrationforJirabyGitKraken"":{""count"":2,""name"":""Git Integration for Jira by GitKraken""}}}}},""isStale"":true}}",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,1

column1: Several times in the last few months we’ve seen Triton builds hang on the unit test portion of the build. The tests themselves do not fail, but simply halt after a certain period of time, however the build continues to spin (for hours until someone notices). What this can result in is builds being backed up until the workers are full and further PR builds are blocked, for instance:

At first, we hypothesized that it’s because of a build kicking off, another commit being made, and concurrent builds happening. However, this does not seem to be the case every single time. Our only recourse at this point is to kill the builds and restart them again.

Based on this it looks like there are the following conditions:
* We cannot use spot instances on zeus orchestrator jobs or HCG/MARa masters since they are statefulsets
* We would need to create new node groups for apps-green since you cant change existing node groups.
* Its recommended we use karpenter for autoscaling with spot instances.
* We might be able to leverage the HCG node group in theory.","24/Jul/24 8:48 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Here is the recommended actions we take:
* Migrate from AWS Cluster Autoscaler to Karpenter (Karpenter is more efficient in managing spot instances out of the box and has overall much more benefits)
* Implement Node Termination Handler (This allows EKS to gracefully drain nodes when AWS is going to stop a SPOT instance)
* Create new SPOT Managed Node Groups to replace our existing ones in DEV-EKS
* Migrate our applications to the new SPOT Managed Node Groups (This is done through deployments changes)
Will review with team if the work is reasonable and create implementation tickets once reviewed.",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,134053,DEVOPS-4874,AWS Cost saving measures,Done,25/Jul/24 8:55 AM

column3: smart-link]","14/Nov/22 12:15 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;So after some reading I came to the following conclusion:

column1: We currently have our EKS cluster set to the default Pod Security Policy with privileged access which means our pods can spin up with access as root without issues.

We installed Datree into our clusters using an admission webhook which is the recommended way of implement dynamic policies into EKS: [https://github.com/datreeio/admission-webhook-datree#:~:text=Overview-,Datree%20offers%20cluster%20integration%20that%20allows%20you%20to%20validate%20your,configs%20associated%20with%20each%20operation.

I verified by trying to deploy a few bad pods which were trying to use elevated privileges and Datree was able to detect this and block their creation using this built in rule: [https://hub.datree.io/built-in-rules/prevent-privileged-containers

For now I believe this is enough for us to consider our future deployment of containers secured.","14/Nov/22 12:37 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;calico-node is using elevated privileges for its network functionality, Im adding a new filter in datree to make sure it doesnt apply the rules on the calico namespace with any resource the prefix of calico","14/Nov/22 2:14 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;kube-proxy is used by AWS to manage communication between the nodes and EKS, I added this to our filter configmap in datree to allow it to deploy any object that starts with the name of kube-proxy in the kube-system namespace.",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,71875,DEVOPS-2881,General Migration of all possible services to the appropriate kubernetes cluster,Done,21/Nov/22 7:58 AM

column1: SPIKE: Allow jenkins workers to share docker cache,DEVOPS-3332,87125,Story,Done,DEVOPS,DevSecOps,software,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,,,Normal,Done,Ari Sela (Artemis),61d9a3429ee70a0068999012,Christian Allred,5d9b608645fad00dc125fe61,Christian Allred,5d9b608645fad00dc125fe61,05/Oct/22 5:20 PM,14/Dec/22 10:27 AM,,27/Oct/22 10:36 AM,,,,,,0,Blocked,planned,,,,,,"What would it take to let the different workers on jenkins share a docker cache? right now if i do work on worker 1, then want to benefit from that work on worker 2 then its not possible. The use case here is the CI / publish steps of ballista....  Right now as part of ballista testing and publication this happens:
* PR made (ci test run, this inclue the building of the production image)
* Publish starts. <- this needs the production image to publish.
** if the publish step happens on a different worker, it can't use the image that was generated in the CI step, so it has to do the work again
Identified best approach for shared docker cache on our jenkins server/workers
* Set up NFS in our worker nodes and configure docker for each one to build the caching into the NFS (Need to further investigate this option)
* Have our images stored in ECR so we can pull them in different steps as needed
* Force the ballista job to use a single node for every step using labels (light lift)
* Configure Jenkins to run executors as containers in single Nodes

It seems that most people are moving Jenkins into Kubernetes and using persistent volumes + ephemeral pods to spin up/down jenkins executors as needed, we have an investigation ticket for moving Jenkins to our EKS cluster in our pileline for Q4 so I want to make sure we arent pulling a heavy lift with this ticket when we are planning to move it out to EKS.

column1: [+_Backing up and restoring an Amazon RDS DB instance_+

{quote}In addition to the daily automated backup, Amazon RDS archives database change logs. This enables you to recover your database to any point in time during the backup retention period, *up to the last five minutes of database usage.*{quote}
RDS uploads transaction logs for DB instances to Amazon S3 every five minutes. To see the latest restorable time for a DB instance, use the AWS CLI [describe-db-instances
column2: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/rds/describe-db-instances.html] command and look at the value returned in the {{LatestRestorableTime}} field for the DB instance. To see the latest restorable time for each DB instance in the Amazon RDS console, choose *Automated backups*.

column7: *_10062_*:*_1_*:*_857436451,,,"02/May/22 7:45 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;Ive created a test instance that has a simple API endpoint which uses sleep of 50 seconds before generating a response.

column1: I also set up nginx in the same ec2 instance to do the job of reverse proxying from port 80 to custom port 5000 for the API endpoint

Finally, I installed locust locally and trying to generate enough calls that will replicate the issue with getting 504/502’s from the nginx application.","04/May/22 12:45 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;After separating the applications into their own EC2 instances I was not able to replicate the issue, below is an explanation of how attempted the replication:
* Created simple python flask API application that contains 2 endpoints and uses g-unicorn to manage requests (same configuration as prod):
** / ← sleep of 5 seconds and returns string
** /json ← sleep of 60 seconds and returns a json of 200,00 items
* Created new EC2 instance using the nginx-modsec AMI base image: {{ami-0fd9e0645c770ea59}}
* Configured nginx to proxy traffic to the flask API application (same configuration as prod)
* Send out concurrent requests to both endpoints using locust stress tester.

I was able to verify that the API endpoint was handling requests as expected and that nginx was erroring out with timeouts all of the json requests since its configured to expire any request that takes longer than 60 seconds to finish.
When looking at the EC2 instance monitoring tools I could not find any peaks of CPU usage or Memory in the TOP command.

Since we can’t replicate this issue we will have to close out the ticket and hopefully if there is another issue in production we can run some forensics on it to better determine the root cause of nginx causing requests times higher than 60 seconds.",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Done,04/May/22 12:45 PM

column8: *_10062_*:*_1_*:*_4565,,,"24/Mar/22 5:44 AM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;We triaged the issue to solve it, here are the steps we took per [~accountid:5c992b27520ecd756a46dd9d] :

column1: # Looked at the nginx auth logs on the loadbalancer (use-dev-lbwaf1/2 -> /var/log/nginx/dev.access.log).  This is where we saw the upstream timeout was exactly 60 seconds - you can see it starts to forward the requests to the other hermes server because it's loadbalanced between use-dev-hermes1 and use-dev-hermes2 - so you start seeing two IP addresses in the response where the upstream hits
# Look at what changes might have happened around that timeframe - [@Ari Sela
column2: https://artemis-health.slack.com/team/U02RT3GV4CC] noticed that the security group configs were different between the two hosts by looking at the security tab in the instance configuration: [https://us-east-1.console.aws.amazon.com/ec2/v2/home?region=us-east-1#InstanceDetails:instanceId=i-0c4f50e50b94b27d9

column1: Went to cloud trail to search for who might have modified that security group during the timeframe: [https://us-east-1.console.aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/home?region=us-east-1#/events?EventName=ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute
Saw that that rat bastard {{mtaylor}} modified it to remove the ""open to the world"" security group for zabbix and graylog

column2: https://artemis-health.slack.com/team/U02RT3GV4CC] added it back and we retested.

column1: The upside is that it's solved - the downside is that the zabbix and graylog group is open to the world, and is used EVERYWHERE - so the communication between the load balancers and the servers themselves is depending on that wide open security group for things to connect properly.",,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,Done,24/Mar/22 5:44 AM

column14: width=1159,height=624!","23/Mar/22 12:45 PM;61d9a3429ee70a0068999012;After reviewing the issue and taking a look in the server (10.0.10.225) we identified the following:

# Server provides it’s host key information and what algorithms it supports for authentication
# User and host negotiate the protocol they’re using and agree after verifying they are who they say they are
# Server requests authentication, and will iterate through available authentication methods - in this case, public key authentication or ssh authentication
# If a public key is available for this user, the server will encrypt a message with the users public key and send this message to the user.
# If the user has the private key that matches the public key, they will decrypt the message, and send a reply with the appropriate response

# Once the server verifies they can decrypt the message, that tells the server they are who they say they are, since they have the private key that’s secret that is used with the public key - it authenticates them and lets the SSH connection proceed

# If there are no public keys, or the public key verification fails for some reason, the server will fall back on alternative authentication methods, like password, where the server will request the password, and if it’s correct, will authenticate the session
# If none of the acceptable authentication methods are correct, the server will close the connection
*This workflow should allow the connection that we should see in the logs if they get to our server at all*

That’s why when we look at the logs, we should at least see a connection attempt to our public IP address - step 1 happens no matter what - regardless of if they have the correct authentication or if it fails authentication, we should always see step 1, because the IP address is publicly reachable with no whitelisting in place.

The verbose logs show us steps 2-8, where the standard logs just show us step 1 and step 9 - and step 2-8 are where we would be able to identify why the connection failed and what methods were attempted when it failed.
Regular auth logs should show us step 1 and 9 as well, regardless of whether or not it was successful.

*The private key is essentially like giving out a password* - that’s why generally speaking I wouldn’t expect them to ever give us the private key, only the public.  ","17/Mar/22 3:47 PM;5d3e8185982c2b0db29871f4;Popped up to a Sev 1, then dropped back to a Sev 3 for this one.

column1: The duplicates happened because there was a bug in our new SFTP script which we ran for all of the month of February which caused files to be uploaded with incorrect filenames.
